title: The post that worked, and why
text:
For six months the bakery posted photos of bread. Beautiful photos, good light, almost no engagement.

Then the owner posted something else: a short video of her hands shaping dough at 4:30 in the morning, with one line of text about why she still does it herself. Reach jumped from 900 to 34,000. Two hundred new followers in a day.

Her marketing friend explained it simply. The bread photos showed the product. The video showed the pain point behind it: everyone who watched was awake at 4:30 for a reason of their own.

The temptation after a post goes viral is to repeat it exactly. She didn't. She built a content calendar around the same idea instead: three posts a week, each showing one real moment from the shop. Not staged, not polished.

Six weeks later the numbers looked different. Reach was lower than the viral post but four times higher than before. More useful, the landing page for the baking course had a conversion rate of 7%, up from under 2%.

One viral post is luck. A format that keeps working is a strategy.

questions.q: Why did the video perform better than the bread photos?
options: It connected with something the audience felt
It was longer and more detailed
It was posted at a better time

questions.q: What did the owner do after the post went viral?
options: Built a repeatable format around the same idea
Paid for ads to boost it

questions.q: What happened to the landing page conversion rate?
options: It fell after the viral post

questions.q: What is the main message of the text?
options: A repeatable format beats one lucky post
Video always works better than photos
Posting early in the morning is best

title: Two hundred euro, four leads
text:
A small language school ran its first paid ads campaign in March. The budget was 200 euro, spread over three weeks, aimed at HR managers in companies with more than fifty employees.

The first version failed quietly. The headline was "Professional English Courses" and the call to action said "Learn more". Click-through rate: 0.4%. Nobody filled in the form.

For the second version they changed two things. The headline became a question the target audience actually asks: "Can your team handle a call in English?" The call to action changed to "See the 20-minute assessment". Same budget, same audience.

Click-through rate rose to 2.1%. Eleven people downloaded the lead magnet, a short PDF with sample assessment questions. Four of them booked a meeting.

The director did the maths. Two hundred euro produced four leads, and one of them signed a contract worth 4,800 euro. The return on investment was obvious, but she noticed something else: the winning ad said nothing about the school. It only described the client's problem.

They now start every campaign with the pain point and add the offer last.

questions.q: Why did the first version of the ad fail?
options: It described the product, not the client's problem

questions.q: What was the lead magnet in this campaign?
options: A PDF with sample assessment questions

questions.q: How many people booked a meeting?
What did the director learn from the winning ad?
options: Lead with the client's problem, not the offer
